Remote reservoir in the upper Tywi valley behind the tallest dam in the UK (91 m). Farms were drowned when it was built in the early 1970s, and Fannog farmhouse's roof shows when the water is low. The spillway roars after heavy rain.

Hideout of the 'Welsh Robin Hood', Thomas Jones (c.1530–1609), on the wooded hill of the RSPB Gwenffrwd-Dinas reserve near Rhandirmwyn, just south of Llyn Brianne. Reached by the reserve's riverside trail and a scramble up the boulders. Position approximate.
A minor spring and pool in Holywell attributed to St Beuno, uncle of St Winefride; the Royal Commission noted only a slight spring here in 1912.
Stone-built well chamber with a twin structure beside a pond inside a polygonal enclosure; much of the setting was dug out after 2001 to make a duck pond, exposing the footings. On private land.
Ffynnon Mihangel / St Michael's Well, Cilcain
Holy well dedicated to St Michael, already ruinous when Edward Lhuyd noted it c.1700; now just a shallow overgrown hollow.
St Mary's well in the south corner of Halkyn old churchyard: a round stone basin recorded by Lhuyd in 1699, now capped with slabs that are probably reused gravestones.
Medieval stone-lined well basin long credited with medicinal water, traditionally linked to Gerald of Wales's journey through the area in 1188.
Spring rising in a natural limestone basin near Caerwys, dedicated to St Michael and listed by Edward Lhuyd c.1699.
Rectangular walled well enclosure about 8 by 4 yards outside Caerwys, recorded by Edward Lhuyd; on farmland.
Ffynnon Fair / St Mary's Well, Cwm Vicarage
Well dedicated to the Virgin by the old vicarage at Cwm, mentioned by Edward Lhuyd around 1700; little is recorded of its present state. Location approximate.
Holy well of St Deifer (Dier), the original patron of Bodfari church; once a resort for sick children, it is now a neglected spring.
Wart-curing well of St Cynhafal near Llangynhafal, praised in a late-medieval poem; the present chamber is a modern rebuild tied to field drainage. On private land.
The strongest of a cluster of cold springs near Trevor, Llangollen, enclosed in a small brick surround and once much visited by sufferers of rheumatism.
Ffynnon Fair / St Melyd's Well, Meliden
Small boundary well between Meliden and Gwaenysgor associated with St Mary and the local saint Melyd; now largely dry.
Medicinal spring by Cwm vicarage named for the paired saints Mael and Sulien; steps lead down to water protected by an old grave slab, renovated in 1772.
Stone-lined spring under a bank on a disused road, walled on three sides, dedicated to St Garmon (Germanus); a cross wall once ponded the outflow.
Sunken slate-lined well enclosure regarded as a sacred well of St Beuno, about 6 by 5 feet and 3 feet deep.
Powerful spring of St Asaph, said in Lhuyd's day to ebb and flow and to rival Holywell in volume, once framed by pillars and driving a mill; now absorbed into a modern reservoir.
Site of the well of St Mordeyrn, patron of Nantglyn church, about 250 yards north of the church; the ground is still damp but no structure survives.
Spring roughly 420m north of St Trillo's church in Llandrillo, Edeirnion, named for the church's saint and shown on 1890s OS maps. Distinct from St Trillo's Chapel at Rhos-on-Sea.
Peat-cut, stone-ended trough fed by clear seepage on open moorland, identified as a site of St Dogfan's well; recorded from air photographs in 2007.
St Mary's Well, Betws Gwerfil Goch
Well dedicated to the Virgin that Lhuyd placed 'a stone's throw from the church' of Betws Gwerfil Goch.
St Mary's Well and Bath, Bodrhyddan

Ornate octagonal well house with cupola and pelican finial plus a balustraded bath in the grounds of Bodrhyddan Hall; it bears a spurious 'Inigo Jones 1612' inscription but seems to be 18th century. Private estate.
Medieval bathing well of St Beuno below the Ffynnon Beuno caves: a walled pool whose overflow spouts through a worn carved stone head. Beside a private house.
Open spring with three stone steps down to the water near Derwen, recorded by Lhuyd in 1698; traditionally a healing well for rheumatism.
Well of St Tysilio noted by Edward Lhuyd in 1698 near Bryneglwys; its precise position is now uncertain (location approximate).
Ruined spring complex near Trefnant with a well, bath house and a dressing room with fireplace, showing its use as a bathing well.
Well of St Sadwrn near Denbigh, recorded by Lhuyd in 1698; a low footstone fronts a chamber protected by rough walling.
Old well near Denbigh noted by Edward Lhuyd in 1698; only the channel that carried its outflow survives.
Well of St Elidan near Cefn-y-wern farm, Llanelidan; it has silted up and its exact site is lost (location approximate).
Spring dedicated to St Mary rising in a field named after it on the Plas Du land, documented in a 1620 survey; no surviving traditions.
Ffynnon y Saint / Saints' Well, Bangor-on-Dee
Spring near Hopyard Coppice, probably the 'Ffynnon y Saint' Lhuyd recorded in 1698 in Bangor Monachorum parish, home of the famous early monastery.
Once a famous spring and a fixed point on the medieval England-Wales boundary, recorded in 1448; now only faint boggy traces.
Well of the former St Peter's chapel, some 450 yards from the chapel site; choked but the spring still runs.
Holy well of St Cynfran, said to have been visited to cure sick cattle; now a sludge-filled basin half ringed by a drystone wall in a hedge bank.
Well named for St Tudno, the 6th-century hermit whose church stands on the Great Orme above Llandudno.
Railed holy well at St George near Abergele, made up of a spring pool and a masonry tank; horses were traditionally brought here to be blessed.
Small half-round stone basin capped with a slab behind a housing estate about 150m from Llanrhos church; rediscovered only in 1993.
Spring feeding the River Asa, recorded by Lhuyd c.1698 and probably dedicated to St Asaph; no structure survives.
St Asaph's well in Eglwysbach, documented from 1648, closed in the 19th century and replaced by a village pump; its overflow still wets the meadow.
Well of St Doged, an enclosed basin covered by two large slabs, listed by Lhuyd in 1698.
Parish well of St Digain at Llangernyw (home of the ancient yew), a slab-lined chamber covered in masonry.
Holy well beside the remote old church of Llangelynnin above the Conwy valley: a walled basin in a ruined well house said to be dated 1622; reputed to cure sick children.
Overgrown well of St Garmon in rough masonry about 500m north-east of the church.
Spring of St Nefydd roughly 300 yards from Llannefydd church.
Spring in a bank once protected by two flagstones, recorded by Lhuyd in 1698; now in a modern brick chamber.
Roadside upland well at 484m by the B4407, in a stone-roofed shelter inscribed 'Yf a bydd ddiolchgar' (drink and be thankful), rebuilt 1846.
Natural spring with no structure, recorded by Francis Jones as a wishing well.
Holy well once enclosed in big drystone walls about 8 feet square; now concreted over.
Possible site of the well of St Brothen by the stream near Llanfrothen church, noted by Lhuyd c.1698 and later described as walled on three sides.
Holy well on the Llŷn pilgrim route to Bardsey, now a pool of probable artificial origin with no visible masonry.
St Mary's well near Boduan, originally three-cornered but now heavily modernised as a tank.
Spring of St Gywer in boggy ground about 650m from Llangower church by Llyn Tegid, once paired with a standing stone, Llech Gower; hard to locate.
Stone-lined well chamber cut into a bank at the corner of a ruined building, below Braich y Saint.
Walled, dilapidated well at the north-east corner of Llyn Glasfryn; legend says a maid named Grassi left it uncovered and its overflow created the lake.
Spring under a ruined house that issues through an iron pipe; no saint is linked to it but its water was thought to be remedial.
Square stone-walled pool on Bron Llwyd hill, probably with steps, used by pilgrims bound for Bardsey.
Spring of St Derfel about 350m from Llandderfel church, once protected by slate and rough masonry forming a small reservoir.
Spring dedicated to St Lleuddad of Bardsey, partly banked and formerly walled; masonry shows when it is cleared.
Ffynnon Gadfan / St Cadfan's Wells, Tywyn
Well of St Cadfan near his church in Tywyn, noted in 1535; converted into two baths with dressing rooms before the 1850s and reputed to cure skin ailments and rheumatism.
Small walled well of St Deiniol just north-east of Llanfor churchyard, whose water flowed through the churchyard.
Roadside well on the Roman road Sarn Helen, named after Elen of the legend; no medieval tradition recorded.
Spring by the presumed chapel of St Garmon, now buried in dense forestry, with scattered stones from a former cover.
Sunken well with stone steps, sharing its dedication with St Mary's church 260m away; an older ruined well is also reported nearby.
Small rubble-lined well of St Pedrog, known locally as 'The Wishing Well'.
Holy well of St Aelhaearn by the church, a medieval basin with stone benches covered by a well house inscribed 'Roofed 1900'; later used for water supply.
Well dedicated to St Cawdraf, now covered by a small modern brick structure on what may be old slabs.
Probable holy well of St Einion (Engan), a water-filled walled basin about 3m square.
Medicinal well in the Tal-y-llyn valley below Cadair Idris.
Spring basin backed by a curved drystone revetment, linked with St Tudwen's church at Llandudwen.
Small D-shaped walled well near Aberdaron with a hinged iron lid, still in use in the 1960s but now overgrown.
Well of St Garmon said to cure rheumatism and skin complaints; later used to supply cottages below.
Well near the pilgrim church of St Beuno at Pistyll, known locally as the 'Holy Well'; no ancient features visible.
Large square walled well enclosure with five steps down, valued for medicinal properties.
Rectangular basin with steps enclosing a natural spring, dedicated to St Rhedyw of Llanllyfni.
Spring flowing into a rock cistern, probably the well of St Tecwyn listed by Lhuyd.
Holy well of St Cadfarch near Llannor, modernised with its water diverted into pipes.
Ornate square stone well house built by the Nefyn Corporation in 1868, with slate inscriptions and a pyramid roof, in Stryd y Ffynnon on the Bardsey pilgrim route.
Round walled well with steps down, traditionally held to have curative powers.
Keyhole-shaped holy well: a covered round chamber that feeds a long boulder-lined pool cut into the slope.
Former well dedicated to St Catherine, noted for curing eye infections; filled in around 1962 when a garage was built.
Walled bathing well with stone seats, main bath and drinking tank, restored c.1890; linked to St Curig and said to cure blindness.
Ancient rectangular well with probably 17th-century steps on three sides near St Mary's church, Bryncroes.
Holy well of St Peris by the old church in Nant Peris, with slate steps around a basin and wall niches; its sacred fish were said to foretell cures.
Stone-walled square enclosure with steps and seats around a sunken basin near Rhiw, probably 17th century.
Well of St Baglan near Llanfaglan, once a stone basin with a wide seat around it; now two low walls and a hollow.
Old well of St Michael on the slope of Mynydd Tyn-y-fach: a boulder-walled trench, its flow partly diverted by a modern cutting.
Spring named for St Patrick with no masonry; legend ties the saint to the nearby coast.
Well and bath of St Enddwyn in rough masonry, probably once roofed, said to have healed the saint herself; now choked.
Pungent sulphur spring beside cottages on the Afon Twrch, a popular local spa in the early 1900s with eisteddfodau held alongside; restored 1920 and 1993.
Medicinal well near Aberffraw; no trace now survives.
Well of St Patrick near Llanbadrig church, where the saint is said to have come ashore; noted for cures, its remains were destroyed by a storm in 1967.
Site of St Credifael's well, once a spring-fed masonry basin by a pond; levelled by 1986.
Holy well of St Caffo near Llangaffo, destroyed when the railway was built.
Cliff-foot spring of St Eilian near Point Lynas, visited on the saint's day, with traces of a possible well chapel. Not the Llanelian-yn-Rhos cursing well.
Healing well of St Seiriol at Pont Clorach where Seiriol and Cybi were said to meet; filled in when the bridge was built in 1840.
Stone-lined spring in the grounds of Llanidan Hall, traditionally St Nidan's well, linked to his church; private estate.
Healing well associated with St Cybi near his church in the Roman fort at Holyhead; legend says it sprang where the saint struck the ground.
Small reputed wishing well connected with Llanddwyn and St Dwynwen; destroyed by reservoir construction.
Site of St Beuno's well at Aberffraw, latterly under a brick pump house; now beneath the road.
Boarded-over well shaft about 160m from the site of Llanddygfael church.
Well dedicated to St Deiniol Fab credited with healing waters. Location approximate.
Healing well of St Cybi opposite Ffynnon Seiriol at Pont Clorach, where the two saints were said to meet each week; its water now mingles with the stream.
Pretty well of St Allgo by a stream 350m from Llanallgo church: a small stone enclosure with benches round a pool.
Alleged holy well of St Cybi, a low angle of walling cutting off a field corner; no known traditions.
Natural rock well on the south side of Cerrigceinwen churchyard, dedicated to St Ceinwen and credited with healing.
Holy well of St Myllin above Llanfyllin, where the saint is said to have baptised by immersion; later a closed parish well.
Traditional meeting place on Trinity Sunday at Arddleen; no longer a public well.
St Eluned's Chapel and Well, Slwch
Scheduled site of St Eluned's oratory and holy well near Slwch Tump outside Brecon, scene of a lively medieval saint's-day festival; now platforms by a damp hollow.
St Mary's well at the foot of steps from the churchyard to the River Banwy, long thought curative; restored in 1990 within a small garden.
Spring on the bank of the Banwy at Llanerfyl whose water was used for baptisms at St Erfyl's church.
Well of St Tydecho, now filled; it once had a carved stone saint's head that has been lost.
Well of St Dogfan once used to cure eye disease; now flows into Lake Vyrnwy.
Sulphur spring found in 1732 by Rev. Theophilus Evans that launched Llanwrtyd as a spa; a later well house stands in the Dol-y-Coed Hotel grounds.
Disused well whose water was formerly used for baptisms at St Michael's church.
Embanked muddy pond inside the Castell Dinas hillfort, traditionally curative for skin diseases.
Copious spring reputed to heal infant ailments, now feeding Lake Vyrnwy.
Spring of St Cadog issuing from an iron pipe in a field wall, with the associations of a medieval holy well.
Well dedicated to Our Lady, once provided with a can on a chain; filled in though the spring still runs.
Open spring rising into a natural stone basin at the foot of a 30-foot rock face near Abbey Cwmhir.
Holy well of St David near Llanddewi Abergwesyn church, recorded in Lhuyd's Parochialia.
Ancient holy well of St Garmon, built round with stone and slab-covered, once used for baptism and bathing.
The 'Fons Tessilian' of a 1202 charter, linked to St Tysilio; concreted over with an inspection cover by 1981.
Medicinal sulphur well above the River Edw in a ruined, probably Victorian stone well chamber.
Two medicinal wells of St Cadfarch facing each other across the road at Penegoes, each in low stone walls.
Chalybeate (iron-rich) spring visited for healing, though without any saintly dedication.
Well of St Issui below the remote church of Partrishow: a drystone, slab-roofed chamber with small niches, where offerings are still left.
Spring at the foot of a rock on Gaer Fawr, frequented on Trinity Sunday.
Holy well of St Cynidr with an open well house of c.1900-1910.
Flagged well with steps and a small modern hut, said to have curative powers.
Holy well said to cure eye complaints, adapted for domestic supply under a concrete slab.
Stone-lined healing well with steps, possibly rebuilt about 1900.
Trinity Sunday gathering place near Llys-y-Cawr, with cock fighting held nearby.
Walled basin on a stream bank, once roofed and used for bathing.
Jacket's Well / St Edward's Well, Knighton
Healing well for sprains and rheumatism; the name is thought to come from Welsh 'iachâd' (healing).
Mineral spring of later repute with an older holy well close by.
Possible holy well shown on the 1891 map, now under the Elan reservoir and perhaps visible at low water.
Holy well on the north side of St Mary's church at Pilleth, credited with curing eye ailments.
St Mary's well in a modern fenced enclosure with a hawthorn beside it; no pre-20th-century fabric visible.
Holy well called Ffynnon Fair recorded by Francis Jones in Partrishow parish; its identification is uncertain.
Curative well of St Cadfan in a recess under the road near the church; its well house was lost to road building.
Holy well described as neglected in 1910; now a modern spring chamber.
Spring about 150 yards from St Dogfan's church, reputed for healing.
Medicinal well on Pen yr Allt common believed to cure sprains.
Partly stone-lined spring much frequented for medicinal water, known as the well of David the smith.
Natural spring once renowned for curative properties, later piped to the rectory.
Former roadside spring of St Silin near Ty'n-llan, now dry; the old chamber was filled in.
Spout well of local repute dedicated to the Virgin; its stone bowl was removed when the Aberystwyth road was built.
Plentiful spring south of the ruined monastic hospice at Llanwddyn (the monks' well).
Traditional holy well of St David.
Slate-lined trench and cistern in forestry near Strata Florida, regarded as a holy well.
Gwenhafdre Uchaf Holy Well, Ystrad Meurig
Unusual pyramid-shaped stone well house with a horseshoe chamber, said to have been used by monks walking to and from Strata Florida.
Holy well beside Llanfihangel Genau'r Glyn churchyard, visited by the sick; a crippled girl was said to have walked away cured shortly before 1911. Basin uncovered in 1975.
Chalybeate spring found in 1779 on the Llanbadarn road and later housed as a drinking fountain.
Healing well of St Cybi; the sick bathed here then slept on the Llech Gybi capstone, and recovery or death was read from the result.
Once-famous well of St Peter at Lampeter that gave its name to the Peterwell mansion; now a stony hollow.
Three wells in a row 1.5m apart, each believed to have different properties.
Healing well near ruined St Teilo's church whose water was drunk from the saint's skull, kept by the Melchior family until the 1920s.
Holy spring once running beneath Capel y Pistyll, a pilgrimage chapel by the harbour where St David is said to have been baptised.
Stone-lined well below St Govan's cliff chapel, famous for curing lameness and eye disease; red clay nearby was used as a poultice. Now dry.
Covered clifftop well with a pump near the site of St Mary's chapel above Chapel Bay.
Spring of St Brynach reputed to heal.
Site of St David's well by the cathedral close, said to have sprung after the saint prayed during a drought; no trace survives.
Spring in a deep rough-masonry chamber with reputed healing powers.
St Mary's Well, St Davids Cathedral
Site of St Mary's well beside Pistyll Dewi outside the cathedral close at St Davids.
Pond by a castle mound thought to mark the medieval well of St Teilo, linked to Llangwathen chapel.
Holy well of St Ceinwen with slight traces of foundations.
Strong spring where a well chapel of St Meugan once stood.
Stone well chamber with a corbelled roof set into a bank; listed by Francis Jones, last reported dry in 1975.
Well of the hermit St Caradog, documented in 1315; concreted over in 1838 under a manhole.
Corbelled well chamber by Llanllawer church famed for curing sore eyes; pins and coins were left as offerings and bent pins thrown in as curses.
Restored walled well in Burton churchyard near a medieval cross base, once used as a baptistery.
Dry well chamber in the rampart of Rudbaxton Rath beside the vanished chapel of St Leonard (recorded 1398).
Stone-lined spring flowing to the sea near the site of Capel Degan.
Water-filled hollow under a masonry hood next to the site of St Brynach's chapel, possibly early medieval.
Spring flowing into a rough basin, said to heal.
Three stone-edged springs in Gumfreston churchyard, two chalybeate and one pure, once visited for their healing water.
Stone well house about 40m from St Justinian's chapel facing Ramsey Island, now supplying a cottage.
Spring probably dedicated to St Aidan (Maedog); largely drained by road widening.
Recently restored, signposted holy well of St Gwyndaf in woodland near Llanwnda church.
Spring reputed for curative powers, though not a traditional sacred well.
Remains of a small walled chamber near St Decuman's church.
Spring 10m west of St Dogfael's church at Felindre Farchog.
Limestone remains of a beehive-shaped well head, the Owen's Well recorded in 1698 near a lost early medieval inscribed stone.
Possibly medieval well of St Brynach near early medieval cross-carved pillar stones.
Curative spring on the St Davids pilgrim route, a small stone-lined cavity disused by 1964.
Corbelled medieval well chamber reputedly supplying Pembroke Castle; possibly a conduit house for St Nicholas's Priory.
Site of a renowned medieval holy well and well chapel with a vaulted chamber.
Former spring of St David, now dry, near Llangwathen chapel.
Corbelled beehive well about 8-9 feet deep close to St Davids Cathedral; door blocked in 1950.
St Mary's well in Cae Ffynnon Fair about 420m from Capel Mair.
Spring of St Celert that once had a well chapel below the church, at the foot of Allt Geler.
Small well chamber of St Brynach, said only to be 'good for sick people'.
Holy well about 300m from All Saints church, later topped by the village pump.
Ruined, possibly 14th-century well chapel at the edge of woodland near Bigawdin farm.
Spring behind Kidwelly Castle, said to have risen where a prince was slain; recorded from 1587.
Healing well near the Dolaucothi gold mines, haunted by Gwenno, who was said to have been imprisoned under the crag by spirits.
Well of St Llawddog by the Teifi near Cenarth church, under a modern brick cover.
Well head with a simple stone arch and an empty niche that once held a saint's image; a pin-wishing well.
Small woodland well near the lost Capel Pen Arw, once highly regarded for cures.
Healing spring linked with St Canna's church and the nearby St Canna's Chair stone.
Well of St Michael beside the site of Capel Mihangel, documented from 1575.
Hillside well where water was drunk with sugar and pins dropped in for good wishes.
Spring of St Tybie about half a mile from Llandybie church.
Five rock pools in Cwm Cerwyni, said to match the five saints of Llanpumsaint church.
Ruined, possibly 14th-century well chapel beside a stream at Banc-y-Mansel.
Churchyard well-baptistery of St Dyfan, visited by pilgrims who stayed at the inn next door.
St James's well close to the site of the vanished Capel Iago.
Spring on Kenfig Burrows in a D-shaped limestone surround, said to be St David's; restored 1985.
D-shaped stone well enclosure partly roofed with slabs, repaired about 1932.
Natural spring venerated as a holy well for curing eye disease.
Tidal underground well near Newton church whose level falls as the tide rises; a miracle-working well and 1920s open-air spa.
Probably a restored medieval well in a walled enclosure near the site of Nottage chapel.
Rubble-stone well chamber of St Sannan with a modern superstructure.
Spring of St Cadog issuing from a pipe in a retaining wall.
Stone-enclosed spring near St Fagans, probably the healing well noted gushing from the rock in 1645.
Covered well in the Cathedral School grounds associated with St Euddogwy, Teilo's nephew.
Probable holy well found in a house cellar on Brecon Road; now filled in.
Lost well in Well Street named after the martyr Tudful, daughter of Brychan.
Medieval vaulted well chamber of St Cybi outside Llangybi churchyard, with interior niches; still intact.
Copious spring of St Ffraid that once filled a walled pool.
Small stone chamber with slab cap, credited with healing; bent pins, coins and buttons were found here in the 1890s.
Fenced well with steps down where King Tewdrig's wounds were said to have been washed before his death.
Horseshoe-shaped walled well with a bench and corbelled niche, popular in the 17th century; rags are still tied to the nearby tree. Guardianship site.
Spring in a drystone setting near Margam Abbey.
Possible holy well of St James near the farm of the same name (location approximate).
Vaulted bath house on the Cwm Bach, possibly first a baptistery for Hen Eglwys and later a cold bath for Margam Abbey.
Spring with trough, probably the well where sickly children were taken in the 19th century.
Lost well at the foot of the rise where St Margaret's chapel stood.
Spring flowing through a stone culvert, perhaps supplying Margam Abbey.
Small vaulted wishing well by the path to Wilcrick church.
Holy well of the Eglwysilan parish (location approximate, given at the farm of the same name).
Stone well house over the spring at Penrhys, a major late medieval pilgrimage centre to the Virgin; restored and still visited.
Spring beside rock-carved figures of 'two saints' recorded in 1696, regarded as a possible holy well or pagan shrine.
Walled spring excavated in 1895 with the remains of the medieval chapel and priest's house in Bishopston valley.
Bubbling spring on Cefn Bryn, perhaps the curative well where pins were left as offerings.
Trinity Well / St Cenydd's Well, Ilston
Well inside the ruined Trinity Well Chapel (c.1649-60, Wales's oldest Baptist chapel) on the site of St Cenydd's medieval chapel.
Walled spring basin of St Teilo used as a garden feature in 1956.
Spring of St Dyfrig with traces of a rubble structure in a hillside recess.
Rectangular stone chamber with a carved panel, linked to the Llanmihangel Place gardens.
Holy well north of St Mary's church at Llanfair, a slab-covered chamber with an attached brick cistern.
Holy well at Beggars Bound, walled and railed.
Roadside well on the way to Peterston reputed to cure eye disorders (location approximate).
Holy well said to cure sore eyes if bathed in before sunrise (location approximate).
Holy well said to cure scrofula (the King's Evil).
Trinity spring near the source of the Afon Alun with possible traces of stonework.
A lime-laden spring by Ridding's Brook near Lymm Dam that turned mosses and twigs to stone, recorded by the Victorian botanist Leo Grindon; exact spot now uncertain, location approximate.
Spring on the edge of Chester known from 18th-century field names; 'Hobby' may echo the hob, a goblin or demon name, hinting at old folklore attached to the water.
Spring beneath the Holy Well Rocks on Alderley Edge whose water was said in the 1840s to cure barrenness; a legend tells of a woman and cow buried by a falling boulder nearby.
Lonely moorland holy well 500 ft up on Harrisend Fell above Scorton, marked on the 1846 map; today just a spring among reeds with no surviving stonework.
Reputed ever-flowing spring near St James's old churchyard, once famed for health, magic and even prolonging life; believed lost to development.
Icy spring above the River Calder below Pendle Hall, once valued as a cure for certain ailments; current condition unknown.

Elegant stone well house built over a spring beside the ruins of Hollinshead Hall near Tockholes, where water pours from a carved lion's head; pilgrims once came for its reputed cure for eye complaints. Reached by woodland paths.
Hilltop well at Preesall described in 1852 as all but deified; rags and clouts were tied to a nearby 'Beggar's Bush' with a prayer for healing.
Spring issuing from a long stone mound at Hardhorn, linked by the Victorian cleric William Thornber to Hallowe'en bonfire cairns and seasonal rites; now largely forgotten.
Cold spring between Hardhorn and Staining that local lore made a favourite haunt of kindly fairies, recorded by Rev. William Thornber in 1837.
One of Preston's earliest wells, at the foot of the Church Street ridge and long a healing and water source; destroyed by later development.
Strong hillside spring rising into a square basin roofed with stone slabs; in medieval times its waters were believed to have special qualities.
Roadside spring in Bowland where generations of travellers, drovers and lead miners stopped to drink; still flowing.
Moorland spring near Kelbrook where Quakers, Baptists and other Nonconformists met for outdoor worship in the 17th-18th centuries, away from parish churches.
Peg o' Nell's Well (St Margaret's Well)

Spring in the grounds of Waddow Hall by the Ribble, beside a headless statue probably of St Margaret; legend makes it the haunt of Peg o' Nell's spirit, whose statue was beheaded to lift her curse. Visible from the riverside footpath.
Marian well beside a shrine chapel at Fernyhalgh, said to have been revealed to a storm-saved merchant in the 15th century; still a Catholic pilgrimage site.
Once a pyramid-roofed well house noted for icy water good for rheumatism and sprains; now capped with an inscribed stone, though parishioners still visit on the saint's day.
Old Burnley well recorded by local antiquarian Clifford Byrne among the holy wells and healing springs of east Lancashire.
One of two old holy wells in Heysham village; its water has been diverted and an iron pump in a stone arch now marks the spot.
Spring trickling into a stone trough, haunted in folklore by Jinny's spirit, who wandered between the well and an old standing stone up the hill.
Holy well at Waterside on the south side of Colne, relocated in recent years by local researchers after its memory survived in the name of the former St Helen's Mill.

Celebrated well in a rugged part of Brindle parish where clear water bubbles through white sand; locals dropped crooked pins in for wishes, and its water was once carted round neighbouring villages for sale.

Healing well near the medieval leper hospital of St Nicholas off Botchergate, prized for curing sores; people still filled 'shaking bottles' there in May in the 19th century. Destroyed by the railway.
Well in Carlisle's old market place linked to St Cuthbert's visit in 685 recorded by Bede; once sheltered by a pillared building called Carnaby's Folly, long since covered over.
Spring at Newton near Gosforth named in a charter of c.1220 as St Helen's Well at the corner of a garden; possibly surviving as a boggy spring above the farm.
Medicinal spring below the limestone cliffs of Humphrey Head, near caves called the Fairy Church and Fairy Chapel; lead miners stayed for days drinking its strange-tasting water to purge poisons.
Once a copious spring of pure water where youths from surrounding villages held games on the second Sunday in May, with nothing stronger than the well water drunk; now only a trickle by a tree.
Spring-fed well by Dronfield church, recorded c.1710 as the source of water for baptising infants; survives with an old stone-lined shaft in the courtyard of a 16th-century forge.
Chalybeate spring, perhaps named for St Anne, where locals made 'Spanish water' with sugar or liquorice on Easter morning; now a disused iron pump, still dressed and blessed each July.
Holy well recorded from 1366, given an arched stone well house by the royalist Hardinge family in 1662; the collapsed arch was later rebuilt by the community.

Well of the Saxon saint Alkmund, recorded from 1190, with steps down to an oval basin in an 18th-century niche; a vicar was reputedly cured by its water and it has been dressed at times. Now railed off in a housing area.
Ever-flowing well beside the rock-cut hermitage at Dale Abbey, which the founding hermit is said to have dug and blessed as holy and a cure for all ills.
Never-failing spring by Silver Well cottage on Ilkley Moor, thought by Victorian writers to have been a holy well, perhaps once given silver offerings; now covered by stone slabs but still running.
Ancient public well near Ladywell House in High Ackworth, probably dedicated to Our Lady; enclosed by the 1890s and now apparently lost, location approximate.
Spring beneath Chapel Hill above the Wharfe, under a hawthorn, where village girls once made wishes; tradition placed a small chapel above it. Now just a boggy patch in the trees.
Well beside Fairy Wood near Nostell remembered in a local poem as a haunt of the little folk, who left when industry came; probable site only.
Chalybeate well in St Helen's churchyard said to have medicinal powers; filled in during the 19th century and now remembered only in local memory.
Sulphurous spring credited in 1831 with curing skin eruptions when applied externally; reportedly filled in during the 19th century and its exact position is now uncertain.
Holy well that once supplied Welton House, possibly the source of the village name; it survives under stone slabs in a copse north of St Anne's College.
Ruined little well house beneath a sycamore, marked on the 1854 map; its fairy folklore is forgotten and water now seeps into a small bog nearby.
Spring bubbling into a small stone-lined chamber on the moors near Pickering, its lintel crudely carved 'Nattie Fontein'; the 'Old Wife' name may recall an ancient earth goddess.
Spring emerging from a blasted rock face into a round trough beside an older square cistern, remembered locally as a wishing well; often choked with litter.
Intensely cold spring near North Hall, long thought good for rheumatism and rickets and once served by a bathing house; covered over by 1846.
Well by St Faith's Lane near the old churchyard, once the only drinking water for the Carrs; filled in c.1820 and its site re-found by a water diviner.
Wishing well tied to the local saint Philip Inglebred, with a stone dated 1667; country girls dropped pins or sixpences in for luck. Now filled in, leaving only boggy ground.
Spring near Grape Lane in Whitby recorded in 1396, later marked by the 'Virgin Pump' on Church Street; now destroyed, its site under a car park.
Well of the 7th-century local saint Everilda in the grounds of Everingham Priory, once open to villagers and praised for abundant excellent water; filled in before 1923.
Seemingly ordinary public well that local lore made Bradford's most supernatural water, haunted by ghosts and black dogs and used for scrying the future at 6 am.
Forgotten holy well below Halliway Banks Wood, recorded as Haliwell Bank in 1490 and reached by its own dedicated footpath on the 1852 map.
Free-flowing, drinkable spring in mossy Shipley Glen, mapped in 1852 as Raygate Well; a hoof-print mark on the rock below gives it its devilish name.
St Peter's Well, Leeds (St Peter's Square)
Intensely cold sulphurous spring at the foot of High Street, used for cold bathing against rheumatism and rickets according to Ralph Thoresby in 1715; long built over.
Deep village well recorded from 1618 under a large slab on Tunwell Lane, a drought-time supply; folklore placed a phantom black dog and a white lady on the lane.
Roadside spring halfway up Carlton Bank whose peat-filtered water was said to have wonderful curative powers, with wishes made while drinking likely to come true; location approximate.
One of Gomersal's main wells, where boys filled bottles with liquorice and treacle on Palm Sunday to make sweet 'Spanish water' and swap tastes.
Copious spring of soft water by Lady Lane near Quarry Hill, close to the medieval Chantry of Our Lady; now lost beneath city buildings.
Town well near the castle under a small steep-roofed conduit house; legend says a local holy man struck the spring from the ground during a drought in 1320-21. Now dry.
Ancient spring in the crypt of York Minster, traditionally where King Edwin was baptised at Easter 627, prompting the first wooden church on the site; no longer open to visitors.
Spring below which Spinkwell House offered health-giving cold baths from 1788; gravestones of 1645 plague victims were built into its well house. Now neglected and muddy.
Clear spring flowing into a stone trough beneath an old hawthorn on Lady Well Lane leading to St Peter's Church; local tradition links it to baptisms by St Paulinus and to Robin Hood.
Spring developed as a cold bath in the early 1700s and rebuilt as a seven-bath spa by Earl Manvers in 1843; the restored bath house opens to the public on volunteer open days.
Clear medicinal spring mapped in 1851, said never to run dry; it flows beneath the Cricketer's Arms opposite, keeping the cellar cool, with a cup-marked stone just above.
One of the most copious springs in England, boiling up into a circular pool by the road near Eshton Hall, recorded with a chapel in 1429; offerings are still tied to nearby shrubs. A listed monument.
Renowned moorland well recorded in 1273 at the meeting point of three townships, famed for never running dry even in 1976; sadly its flow has since failed.
Iron-rich spring trickling from an old stone trough beside New Edge above Colden, staining everything rust-red; such waters were valued for the blood and fatigue.
Walled chalybeate spring off Parliament Street rediscovered c.1792, locally valued as an eye-wash for sore eyes before becoming one of Harrogate's spa wells; now lost.
Holy well 'of some repute' by the old Chapel Idne at Sennen Cove, whose water features in the Arthurian legend of the battle of Vellan-druchar; now lost, probably one of two mapped springs.
Holy well in a valley north of St Michael's church, recorded in 1914 and visited in 1980; by 1998 only a natural basin by a small bridge remained.
Noted spring south of St George's church in Wilton, Taunton, where the afflicted came for cures said to be marvellous; its site was already uncertain by 1873, location approximate.
Renowned holy well behind Logierait church; tradition says its spirit was so offended when the saint's-day market on 22 August was stopped that the water vanished.
Well by the medieval monks' ferry over the Tummel, dedicated to St Bride so travellers could seek her protection, usually by dropping in a brass pin or coin; lost about a century ago.
Well in Blairgowrie's Wellmeadow where tradition says St Ninian camped, drank and baptised converts; later covered over and piped into the town drains.
Whooping Cough Well (Sput na Fruith-chasd), Strathtay
Spring spouting from a high rock by the Tullypowrie Burn, resorted to for curing whooping cough and counted among the three most important wells of the Tay valley; now overgrown.
Whooping-cough healing well in the hills above Comrie, recently revived and signposted by locals; its little pool is full of smooth white quartz pebbles left as offerings.
Spring of excellent water at the foot of the 'Bank of the Gate' below the old Clan Ross castle site; the Ordnance Survey found it under the sea at high tide.
Clear iron-bearing spring in remote Glen Prosen, reached by a straight stone-lined path from a ruined 17th-century chapel; a scatter of quartz stones may once have ringed it. Still drinkable.

Roadside chalybeate well between Broadford and Heaste where travellers drank from a pewter mug; fishermen took its water to pregnant women in Elgol. Recently cleared, with a tin mug left at the roadside.

Holy well and pool beside the Spey behind the Duff family mausoleum; pilgrims came on the first Sunday in May, leaving a stone offering, and its water was said to cure whooping cough, eye and joint troubles.
Holy Well by Loch ma Naire, Strathnaver
Lost holy well near Loch ma Naire, where crowds came twice yearly before sunrise to bathe, walk round the loch, drink from the well and throw in coins for cures; location approximate.
Well on the old road to Ayr, famous in the 17th century for curing 'unthriving children', with crowds gathering especially at May Day; covered over in the 1950s.

One of Earlston's old 'verter' (virtue) wells, a sulphurous moorland spring whose 'gunpowder'-tasting water a local farmer credited with curing a serious internal complaint; lost in the 1800s, location approximate.

Well beside the church in the village that tradition claims as St Patrick's birthplace, used for baptisms and by villagers for centuries until closed in the 1890s; a later fountain nearby carried the name.
Cold spring by Holywell Farm reputed to cure scurvy and other skin diseases and to help rheumatism, used for water until the 1920s; now a boggy patch.
Spring beyond Bracebridge Pool in Sutton Park, once under a well house and much frequented in the 19th century; probably originally dedicated to St Mary. Now a stone-lined hole.
Holy well, first linked to St James's chapel, where pagan-style rites drew a reprimand from Bishop Hugh of Lincoln in the 12th century; later a pilgrimage site whose water served a leper hospital.
Chalybeate well by the Water of Leith, given a well house c.1818 where visitors paid a penny a drink; analysed as rich in iron salts, but destroyed in the 19th century.
Slow chalybeate spring on the west side of Banbury, still often visited in 1841 and leaving a red deposit in its stone channel; built over later in the century.
The 'Haliwelle' recorded c.1100 that named Holywell Lane and the medieval priory, once sweet and frequented by scholars on summer evenings but spoiled by 1603; long destroyed.
Holy well near Holywell Farm, probably linked to the Knights Hospitallers who held Winkburn manor; its water was said to be good for sore eyes. Now an overgrown muddy patch.
Well beside a stream just north-west of an old church site in Co. Wicklow, probably dedicated to St Brigid; still visible in 1927 but now in woodland and condition unknown.

Spring beside the overgrown ruins of a chapel by the Machany Water, so venerated that the Presbytery ordered the chapel demolished c.1650 to suppress the 'superstitions' practised there; now a boggy seep.
Plentiful spring of St Serf, patron of Monzievaird, where on Lammas Day people drank and left white stones, spoons or rags; now drowned beneath the waters of the loch at Ochtertyre.

Gushing roadside mineral spring in Glen Lyon with a stone shelf for offerings, usually small pebbles, which were said to be replaced as fast as roadmen cleared them; offerings were still remembered in recent times.
Holy well of St Mary that gave Tibbermore ('great well') its name, near a church once held by the Bishops of Dunkeld; its site in a roadside paddock now shows no trace.
Holy well by a lost chapel and burial ground on the banks of the Ordie, where locals drank on the first Sunday of May until the 19th century; destroyed c.1850, site now in forestry.
Boggy remnant of a holy well beside the lost chapel site just east of the Dunruchan standing stones; one of two St Patrick's wells in Muthill parish.
Holy Well of Inchadney (Beltane Well), Kenmore
Quartz-edged well near a vanished church of the 'Holy Women', visited by crowds on Beltane morning until the mid-19th century; cleaning in 1914 turned up coins, buttons and a cross-marked stone.
Spring south of the manse famed in pre-Reformation times for miraculous cures and protection against plague and witchcraft; still flowing from a wooded bank in 2014.
Strong cold spring gathering into a clear pool amid gorse in the Ochil foothills, mapped in 1860; no recorded traditions survive.

Trickle collecting in a small stone pool beneath the crags of Weem Wood, once called St Cuthbert's Bath; later named for Sir David Menzies, who restored it and lived as a hermit in the nearby cave. Plaque and modern cross mark it.
Quartz-lined holy well by the river at Callander, mapped in 1862 though overlooked by Scottish holy well surveys; still holding fresh water.
Fine stone-bordered spring below fairy-haunted Maiden Castle, said never to fail; legend says a princess imprisoned in Castle Campbell was allowed out to drink here.

Healing spring said to have moved from the top of Dundurn hill to its foot in disgust; in 1791 seventy invalids came on 1 May and 1 August, walking sunwise three times, bathing, casting white stones on the saint's cairn and leaving rags. Especially sought by the childless.
Clootie well near the high-water mark below the ruined St Bennet's Chapel, where the sick drank and hung rags as offerings; in the 1930s wishers still left a scrap of clothing on the branches.
Holy Well of Isle Maree, Loch Maree
Well of St Maelrubha on a sacred island in Loch Maree, famed for curing insanity; beside it stood a wishing tree so studded with hammered-in coins that it died. Reached only by boat.

Cold spring on the sunny slopes of the Greyfriars' meadows north of the Howff, dedicated by the friars and reckoned the favourite of Dundee's holy wells; repaired after the Reformation but long since lost.
Bright spring flowing from under the Chapelshade braes near the old Chapel of Our Lady, recorded in 1409 and later feeding the town's water supply; now drained beneath the Ladywell roundabout.
Natural spring at the foot of a bank near Lethnot church, where silver coins left as votive offerings were found in the 19th century; the parish name may come from a word for a sacred place.
Well by Menmuir church named for St Aidan of Lindisfarne, believed to cure asthma and skin diseases; drained in the 19th century, though water still issues from a roadside spout.

Old wishing or holy well of Monifieth on the north side of the A92 at Balmossie Bridge, marked by a stone set up by Thomas Erskine in 1847 on the supposed medieval site, inscribed 'Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again'.
Holy well below Airth Castle whose visitors were hauled before the kirk session in 1657 for leaving money, walking in silence and keeping the water from touching the ground; now destroyed.
Ancient well in an old stone well house that gave its name to the St Ninians district of Stirling, beside a demolished chapel recorded from 1242.
Healing spring high on the boggy moors above Balmaha, overlooking the islands of Loch Lomond; the village name is thought to come from the same saint.
Holy well at the northern foot of Gowan Hill below Stirling Castle, drawn by J.S. Fleming in 1898; built over and destroyed in the 20th century.
Airthrey Mineral Wells, Bridge of Allan
Cold mineral springs below the Ochils, noted by Defoe as useful against skin complaints, whose fame turned Bridge of Allan into a Victorian spa town; the old well house survives as a ruin.
'Very fine well' at the foot of Dumyat rising from over sixty springs through sand, described in 1792 as much resorted to by Catholics; still runs clear.
Called the most famous of Stirling's holy wells, a village water supply and ritual site whose customs drew repeated church complaints; now marked only by a notice board.
Well where local people practised healing rites condemned in old church records, probably the 'Christ's Well' of Menteith described in 1618 as hung all about with rags; exact location disputed.

Lonely spring in Touch Glen near Gilmour's Linn whose virtue lasted one hour a year: drinking at sunrise on the first Sunday of May was believed to preserve your life for twelve months. Long reduced to a boggy spring, location approximate.
Holy well of the saint who gave Kinglassie its name, sheltered by hawthorn and elder; the spring has been piped and bricked for water supply.
St Andrew's Well, Isle of May
Walled spring beside the Altar Stones on the Isle of May, the island's best water and its main domestic supply, though prone to drying in summer.
Small spring by the mill dam at Gateside beside the supposed site of St Mary's Chapel, remembered as a source of holy water before the Reformation.
Tobar Mor (Well of the Winds), Gigha

Magical well on Cnoc Largie kept by an old woman guardian who, for silver, would clean it with a white clamshell, stir it sunwise and fling water toward the wind wanted by sailors; left uncovered it was said it could flood the island.
Tobar na h-Aoise (Well of Age), Iona
Natural pool near the summit of Dun I on Iona, the 'well of eternal youth', where pilgrims came at dawn to touch the water as the first sunbeam struck it to renew their youth.
Tobar na Gaoithe Tuath (North Wind Well), Iona
Lost magic well north of Cnoc nam Bradhan near the Hermit's Cell, where sailors left offerings to summon a north wind; location approximate.
Tobar nam Buadh (Well of Virtues), St Kilda
Exceedingly cold spring near the Amazon's House on Hirta, described by Martin Martin in 1703 as a cure for colic, gravel and headaches; votaries once left humble offerings on a stone altar beside it.
The most northerly healing well on mainland Britain, a stone-surrounded spring with two troughs that also served the keepers of Dunnet Head lighthouse, who carried its water half a mile uphill.
Spring by the Loch of Boardhouse in Orkney once believed to be the home of a trow, the island troll; its folklore is now forgotten but the spring still flows.
Woodland 'well of the old woman' on Cairds Hill, once known for curing ailments and linked to a tale of the Cailleach bathing here and emerging young; still running as a dammed pool.

Celebrated healing spring on Ilkley Moor, enclosed c.1760 by Squire Middleton in a white bath house with plunge baths for the 'cold water cure'; the building is open and water still runs into a plunge pool.

Copious pure spring at the edge of Hildenley Wood near Malton running into a small well house and pool, said to have been much used by the monks of Kirkham Abbey and still credited with healing virtues in 1859.
Ancient healing spring by St Helen's Beck in Chapel Wood near the Wharfe, close to a lost chapel and cross at St Helen's Ford; reputedly haunted and venerated since pre-Roman times.
Medicinal holy well by St Helen's Bridge in Holbeck, once beside a chapel, later known as the Holbeck Spa Well; lost to industrial Leeds.
St Lambert's 'fountain', recorded in the 12th century and probably in the present churchyard; it is thought to have given its name to the Halikeld ('holy spring') wapentake.
One of the springs that named the village of Well, where an iron cup once hung for travellers; a Roman bath house stood nearby.
Spring of excellent water on the former Holy Well Lane, where local people once left 'memaws' — rags, coins and flowers — as offerings to the water.
Moorland well where people bathed their faces to cure poor sight and eye complaints, hanging rags on an old rowan tree as offerings; now under a water-authority cover.
Well near the Monk Pits recorded by Ralph Thoresby in 1715 as long esteemed a sovereign remedy for sore eyes; lost to the growth of Leeds in the 19th century.
Healing well in the East Field near Spring Cottage Farm where villagers bathed sore eyes; long lost, location approximate.
Chalybeate spring with May Day traditions, enclosed in a spa house and prominent in Calderdale's history from the late 18th to late 19th century.
Sulphur spring under a small well house dated 1666, said in 1765 to have been used 'time out of mind' for healing.
Well with a stone trough near Howbalk Lane end, haunted by the 'Hawklemass Ghost', which village youths dreaded passing after dark.

'Excellent spring' at Lee Hall where the lady of the hall dipped children with rickets on Whitsun, Midsummer and St Peter's Eves, said to bring either a speedy cure or death; exact spot lost, location approximate.
Well in the Far-well Field beside the site of St Helen's Chapel, recorded c.1200; still visible in 1823 but now gone.
Well in a small railed amphitheatre, enclosed in 1932, which legend says Bede's monks visited from Jarrow for water; now dry after its spring was diverted by shipyard slag works.
Wishing well at the foot of Worm Hill tied to the Lambton Worm legend, where crooked pins were offered and Midsummer Eve festivities held; reportedly restored in 1974.
Spring flowing from a rock on the old parish boundary path above Looe, much used by villagers for its excellent water before being enclosed in a shed and piped to the town.
Rock basin just below the porch of St Winwaloe's church on the shore at Gunwalloe, filled with sand at every high tide; already ruined by 1875.
Scheduled well in a small well house, said to be a powerful wishing well for divining love, though some locals avoided it as a haunt of mischievous pixies.
Spring in a dip by the stream near Barrow Wood, long visited to bathe sore eyes; a dedicated cup was kept there for drinking.
Three sacred springs outside Derry's walls named in the annals for Adomnán, Martin and Columba; already declining by 1837, now gone.
St Patrick's Well, Grianan of Aileach
Well between the outer ramparts of the Grianan of Aileach where Patrick is said to have baptised Prince Eoghan; pilgrims once pushed pins into a tree beside it.
Virgin Mary's well by the Braid Burn, praised in 1792 for its large flow and light, wholesome water; now lost.
One of a ring of sacred and healing springs around Arthur's Seat, renowned for its water; disrupted when the railway cut into the hill, site approximate.
Sweet spring seeping from beneath a lichen-covered boulder below the Druid's Altar crag near Bingley, near the lost 'Altar Well'.

Overgrown stone ruin of a reputed spring beside the path through Pittencrieff Glen, dedicated to William Wallace; in 1773 the council fought to keep the townsfolk's right of access to the 'Well of Spaw'.
Holy well by the Dam Brae, attached to the vicarage of St Michael's church and celebrated in 1857 for the excellence of its water.
Little-known healing well on the slopes of Arthur's Seat, still running clear into a stone trough by the path; its name may recall coin offerings.
Holy well of the dragon-slaying archangel near the Cowgate and St Mary's Street, shown on a sketch of the city c.1540; possibly remembered in the later 'Silverwell Close'. Long gone.
Remote spring on a steep slope in Snaizeholme valley whose name may recall the Cailleach or old earth goddess; known only from place-name records.
Well beneath Wharncliffe Crags where the legendary seven-headed Wharncliffe Dragon was said to drink, close to the Dragon's Den and the 'Old Wife's Cellar'.
Healing spring of wide renown off Manningham Lane, with a Wart or Pin Stone beside it; now under or beside Valley Parade football ground.
Well near Kettleness where fairies were said to wash their linen and beat it with bittle and pin, the noise carrying a mile on fairy washing nights.

Black Isle rag well linked by some to the Virgin Mary, formerly visited on the first Sunday of summer; cloots were still being tied to nearby trees when recorded in 2014, though tree roots are toppling its stones.

Medieval well dedicated to the Anglo-Saxon archbishop St Plegmund, possibly marking his hermitage; long known locally as a christening well. A scheduled monument, restored in 1907, though now without water.

Stone-lined well chamber with steps down to the water, said to mark where King Oswald fell at the battle of Maserfelth; coins and objects were left here for healing. Scheduled monument, well kept by the community.
Chibbyr Undin (Well of the Ash), Grenaby
Manx healing well near Grenaby: the sick drank, walked sunwise round it two or three times, then hung a wetted rag from their clothing on the hawthorn, expecting a cure as the cloth rotted.

Cliff-top spring above the sea by Maughold churchyard, said to be blessed by St Maughold; drinking while seated in the saint's rock chair was thought to help, especially women. Pilgrimage on the first Sunday in August; now a few tumbled stones.
St Winefride's Well, Holywell Farm, Clutton

Large circular stone basin fed by several springs, one of a chain of wells said to mark the route of St Winefride's relics from Holywell to Shrewsbury; a medieval pilgrim station, its worn coping shows long use. Scheduled; in a private farm garden.

Medieval dressed-sandstone well basin by the brook dividing Rainhill and Sutton, reputed in the 19th century to cure eye complaints; its stone figure of a woman with a pitcher is long lost. Scheduled, partly silted.
Simple medieval roadside spring beside Southport Road, covered by an oval capstone carved with a small floriated cross and linked to the nearby wayside cross; a rare Lancashire survival. Scheduled.

Pilgrimage well near Doon Rock, the O'Donnell inauguration site, said to have been blessed by a fasting priest; pilgrims make barefoot rounds and bathe limbs, and two rag trees hold medals, rosaries and other offerings. Well maintained and still busy.

Clifftop wellhouse on St Declan's Way above Ardmore Bay, topped by worn crucifixion carvings; pilgrims make three rounds and drink the water, reputedly good for sore eyes, with a candlelit pattern on 24 July.

St Brigid's well near the ruined Black Abbey at Tully outside Kildare town, still a place of devotion; families traditionally came on her feast day, 1 February, to pray for health and fertility for household, stock and crops.

Group of rock-cut wells beside a great ash rag tree near Kells: one side of the healing well cures headaches, the other toothache, and a stone 'chair' eases back pain. Thousands attended its harvest-time pattern in the 1910s; three magical trout are said to appear.
Holy well in Marown parish in the island's central valley, recorded among the Manx sacred springs on the Megalithic Portal.
Holy well by the ancient Lonan Old Church, listed among the island's sacred springs on the Megalithic Portal.
Manx holy well recorded among the sacred springs of the Isle of Man on the Megalithic Portal; little tradition is recorded.
Chibbyr Pherick (St Patrick's Well), Peel Hill

Well on the seaward side of Peel Hill below Corrin's Tower, said to have sprung where St Patrick's horse first touched land; drinking before sunrise on Old May Day with a wish was thought to make it come true, and silver was once left. Location approximate.
Medieval well in the churchyard at Kirkandrews-on-Eden, probably once used for baptisms.
Well by St Cuthbert's church at Edenhall, source of the legend of the 'Luck of Edenhall': fairies disturbed while drinking here are said to have left behind a medieval glass cup.
Holy well at Great Asby in a stone enclosure probably of the 19th century; a Grade II listed structure.
Well near St Michael's church at Arthuret, its structure probably dating from the 17th century.
Ancient well with a 19th-century wellhead restored by Sarah Losh; well and wellhead are Grade II listed.
Medieval well near St Mungo's church, Bromfield, with a listed wellhead built in 1878.
Roadside holy well by Ullswater linked to St Patrick, sheltered by an 18th-century well house; the original spring may have been slightly elsewhere.

Probably 15th-century granite well head beside St Petroc's church, Bodmin, its roof imitating slate courses; a carved panel shows St Guron, said to have founded a hermitage here in the 5th century, kneeling at the well. Grade II*.
Small 15th-century granite well house on the Lizard, restored in the 19th century, keeping its corbelled roof, seat ledges and an empty niche; its gable cross is now in Grade church. Scheduled.

Holy well by a ruined chapel in the dunes, where pilgrims bathed their feet in water thought to have miraculous powers; lost to sand, re-excavated in 1911 and 1923, its basin still brims with clear water.
15th-century well house in a cobbled courtyard by Luxulyan church; dried up when a tramway cutting diverted its stream, but local people still leave fruit, flowers and candles inside. Scheduled.
Small medieval well house built into a bank with a granite slab roof and steps down to the water, inscribed as restored in 1852. Grade II.

Well said to have sprung where the Anglo-Saxon virgin St Urith was beheaded with a scythe; sufferers of eye disease came to anoint themselves after St Peter's day, and pilgrim offerings helped build the church tower. Now a capped drystone well. Grade II.
Mineral spring on the Water of Leith found c.1760 and compared to Harrogate water; in 1789 it was housed in a round Doric temple by Alexander Nasmith with a statue of Hygeia, restored in 1888.

Artesian spring south of the Glasgow Necropolis in Dennistoun, older than the city itself, which stayed open as a public well after piped Loch Katrine water closed most others; reputedly Glasgow's last public well.
Triple spring in Totnes whose outlets are named Toad, Long Crippler and Snake, feeding three basins reached by three lanes; long used for healing, with a strong emphasis on the number three.
Chalybeate spring in the grounds of the old Bishop's Palace at Bromley, reputed to heal and once a pilgrimage site with an oratory to St Blaise, patron of the wool trade.
Spring beside the River Irvine at the Golffields footbridge, also called St Anne's Well or the Spoot, perhaps a corruption of St Inan's Well; marked by a 1994 plaque.
Shallow alcove well set into the wall of Chapel Lane by the River Irvine, with a plaque reading 'St Inan's Well AD839'; coins are thrown in for luck.
15th-century spring well at the foot of Kirk o' Shotts church, where legend says the giant Bertram de Shotts was hamstrung and killed as he lay down to drink; restored in the 2000s.
14th-century limestone well house built for Llanthony Priory's manor at Hempsted, carved on the back with St Anne, the Virgin and an angel; now dry. Grade I.

Spring said to have gushed up where St Winifred's relics rested in 1138, famed among pilgrims for healing broken bones, with a second spring for eyes; red-spotted 'bloodstained' pebbles appear in it. Timber-framed well house above.
Rare surviving holy well house over a spring below Greenhill Farm; its water was thought to protect travellers and ensure their safe return. Category B listed.
Possible holy well beside the Carmel Water below Kilmaurs Place, a public supply recorded in 1709 famed for never drying up; it stopped flowing in 2013.
'Well of the cliff' near Lough Gill, an ancient spring said to have been a pagan gathering place and later a Penal-era Mass site, with a reputed healing stone nearby.
Almost intact late-medieval granite well house over a spring near Callington, dedicated to St Ethelred; its water was believed to cure whooping cough.
Spring rising into a sandstone basin among elder trees at Blymhill Marsh, famed as a remedy for eye complaints; it was once dressed annually with flowers and branches amid rustic games.
Sandstone well on Mill Lane, Wavertree, dated 1414 and once topped by a cross, inscribed in Latin warning that the Devil laughs at anyone who gives nothing; alms supported the monks. Grade II.

Never-failing spring at the source of the River Sheppey where St Aldhelm is said to have sat singing psalms on the day he died in 709; pilgrims bathed for healing, and flowers and offerings are still left.

Town well on Well Lane fed by four springs through lead spouts into a granite trough, recorded from the 14th century and said never to run dry; it had healing repute and a stone that brought luck in marriage to women who touched it.
Walled holy well with a cross slab in Castlegar East near Ahascragh, protected as a National Monument; a pattern was held here on 15 October.

Spring by the Stra Burn ford near Auchmannoch House marked by a large inscribed red sandstone cross; remembered as a curative, wishing and clootie well where Mary Queen of Scots supposedly watered her horse.

Well beside the ruined church and rock 'seat' of St Fillan at Kilallan near Kilmacolm, site of the 7th-century cell of a saint so revered that his arm bone was carried before the Scots army at Bannockburn.
15th-century well house in a wooded valley at St Austell, restored after the First World War by Admiral Graves-Sawle in memory of his son; drop in a pin and make a wish, and it will be granted.
Spring-fed pool in a stone ring near Dumfries where coins and pins were left and ribbons tied to bushes in 1892; rags and offerings are still left today.
Large bubbling basin beside a 12th-century church and an ancient cross west of Clonmel, visited by pilgrims for cures, especially of headaches; said never to freeze.
Holy well reached by steps above Hatchery Lane, once the water source of the Augustinian priory, its well house built with salvaged priory carvings; the saint's day on 9 June was celebrated here.
Three holy wells by a 7th-century church site on Tara Bay — one for washing hands, one for eyes, one for drinking — a major pilgrimage site from the 13th century, restored by the parish in the 1970s.
Group of four holy wells with men's and women's bath houses east of Downpatrick, linked to St Patrick and still visited for cures; a chapel is recorded in 1306 and the buildings date from c.1600.

Ancient holy well beside St Cuthbert's Church, Bellingham, which the saint is said to have found; a miraculous cure is told of a girl who drank from it. Water now runs through a Georgian 'pant' and is still used for baptisms.
St Ann's Well, St Anne's Park, Raheny
Holy well under a stone hood in St Anne's Park, which takes its name from it; it dried up in the 1950s and remains dry, though the opening was cleared and grilled in 2018.

Holy well on the site of St Gobnait's 6th-7th-century nunnery near Ballyvourney, with a circular path for praying the rounds and a 1951 statue of the saint by Séamus Murphy; still a popular pilgrimage site.
Sir John Schorne's Well, North Marston

Village well blessed by the rector Sir John Schorne c.1290, which became a great pilgrimage resort after his death, its offerings paying to raise the church nave; renovated in 2004-05. Location approximate.
St Cubert's Holy Well (cave), Holywell Bay
Holy well in a sea cave at Holywell Bay, emerging near a cleft in the rock through which children were passed to cure rickets. Tidal access; location approximate.
15th-century granite well house near St Cleer churchyard, built with a 'bowssening' pool for total immersion, with an old cross beside it.
St Clether Holy Well and Chapel
Holy well and small chapel west of the church, among the best preserved in Cornwall, dedicated to St Clether, one of the children of the Welsh king Brychan.

Spring in a small tree-covered moated enclosure north-east of Woolpit church, named 'Our Ladys Well' in the 1570s and probably a medieval pilgrimage site linked to the church's shrine of the Virgin; a scheduled monument and nature reserve.
Spring said to have risen where a bird dropped the arm of the slain King Oswald, believed to cure eye trouble and possibly sacred before his time. Location approximate.
Holy well at the foot of a small cliff about 100 m south of the ruined oratory of Temple Cronan in the Burren, probably named after St Cronan. Location approximate.
Sacred spring said to have burst out when St Maolrubha tore a small tree from the ground, beside the rock he used as a pulpit; now under a stone well house, with a cross-marked stone found nearby.
Holy well outside the church at Burton Dassett, in a stone well house, which still provides water.
Holy well beside St Kentigern's church, Caldbeck, where Christians are said to have been baptised in the 6th century. Location approximate.
Holy well beside the 15th-century St Piran's Chapel among farm buildings at Trethevy, covered by a mid-20th-century slate beehive topped with an iron cross.
Well halfway down the cliff west of Morwenstow church, said to have gushed out where St Morwenna rested while carrying a stone up for her church; now dry, in a Grade II well house.

Mineral-spring well first recorded in 998, used by monks and long the town's main supply; water pours into the river through carved stone gargoyle mouths and was said to cure eye complaints. Restored 2005-07; scheduled.
Holy well of Saxon origin near St Mary's church, covered by an octagonal structure built by the rector in 1764; Grade II listed. Location approximate.
Holy well beside the ruined church that gave Kiltubbrid ('church of the well') its name; folklore says it sprang up anew nearby after being filled in. Location approximate.
Reputed holy well in Kilkeasy graveyard where the 'healing water', said to cure warts and sore eyes, collects in a hollow in a tree. Location approximate.
Holy well near the ruined parish church that gives Tybroughney (Tiobra Fhachna, 'Fachtna's well') its name; a pattern was held on 13 February, feast of the hermit St Modomnoc. Location approximate.
Spring at the end of the mill pond in the hamlet of Chadwell, fed from a small clear pool across the road and described by Hope as approached by old stone steps.
Ruined Neolithic passage-grave on a hillside ledge near Bethel, built in several phases from about 5,000 years ago - a style more usual in Ireland. In Cadw care with open access.
Two Neolithic chamber tombs just north-west of Bodedern near Llyn Llywenan; the southern one still holds a 4m capstone on stout uprights. Cadw site, free access across a field.
Cracked 4m capstone resting on three uprights on a rock outcrop near Llanfaelog, once covered by a cairn and excavated in 1935. In Cadw care.
A collapsed Neolithic dolmen north-east of Llanfairpwllgwyngyll whose 3.6m capstone has slipped onto its supports; a sill stone hints it was once a passage grave.
Partly collapsed Neolithic tomb on a scrubby hilltop above Benllech, where excavators found the remains of 56 people. The capstone now rests with one end on the ground.
Two huge quartz-rich boulders, up to 4m tall, with a fallen 5.5m slab between them, near Llangristiolus - debated as a tomb or a natural glacial jumble.
A neat little mushroom-shaped cromlech on a hillock at Bodowyr Farm east of Llangaffo, admired by antiquarian Henry Rowlands in the 1700s. Cadw site in a farmer's field, open access.
Collapsed capstone in a field west of Brynsiencyn, drawn standing in 1723 by Henry Rowlands; some argue it is just a big boulder. Excavated in 2014.
Squat Neolithic tomb near Moelfre with a 25-tonne capstone on low uprights over a pit chamber; bones of 15-30 people were found in 1909. Cadw site beside the lane.
Three successive Neolithic chambers under one cairn on a knoll near Trearddur, Holy Island, excavated 1977-79. A line of small stones leads towards Tŷ Mawr standing stone; Cadw site.
Tall Bronze Age standing stone in a field on Holy Island, a few hundred metres from Trefignath. In Cadw care.
Bronze Age standing stone in farmland near Llantrisant, Anglesey. A Cadw guardianship site.
About 3.1m tall Bronze Age stone near Amlwch; early writers mention a second upright and a capstone that have since vanished.
Three standing stones set in a triangle in a field near Llanfechell, north Anglesey - an unusual prehistoric arrangement.
The 'thief stone' near Rhosybol: a 1.6m standing stone with a distinct hump on one side that has given rise to local folklore about a petrified thief.

Bronze Age burial mound by the Afon Alaw; when a cremation urn turned up in 1813 it was hailed as the grave of Branwen from the Mabinogion. Excavation in 1967 found a ring cairn, central stone and several urns.
The tallest standing stones in Wales, nearly 4m high, near Brynsiencyn - survivors of a ring of eight torn up by treasure-seekers in the 1790s. Cadw site.
Circular bank near Brynsiencyn that began as a probable Neolithic henge or sanctuary and was later refortified. Maintained by Cadw.
Double-banked pentagonal enclosure by the Afon Braint west of Brynsiencyn, probably Iron Age with Roman-period use. Cadw site.
Walled late-Roman native village of round and rectangular stone huts in woods near Moelfre, where iron was worked; near Lligwy Burial Chamber. Cadw, open access.
'Arthur's Table' - a flat-topped limestone hill above Red Wharf Bay ringed by a stone-walled Iron Age fort, with the tiny church of St Michael beside it.
Iron Age fort on the cliff-girt summit of Bryn Ddiôl near Marian-glas, with sea views; the gentle western approach is cut off by ramparts.
Wales's most northerly hillfort, on a headland near Llanbadrig and Cemaes, partly defended by sheer cliffs.
Small lake near RAF Valley where over 150 Iron Age metal objects - including a slave gang-chain - were found in 1942, apparently thrown in as offerings.
Holy well of St Allgo near Llanallgo church, Moelfre, enclosed by stone walls. Scheduled monument.
Coastal Iron Age fort on a glacial mound above the beach south of Caernarfon, half lost to sea erosion; linked in the Mabinogion with Lleu Llaw Gyffes.
The largest and strongest hillfort in Arfon, near Llanddeiniolen, with a stone wall inside two massive earth ramparts up to 9m high.
Rocky 263m hill above Porthmadog crowned by an odd fort with many white quartz stones in its wall, perhaps religious rather than military. Paths from the Black Rock Sands road.
Iron Age hillfort enclosing the summit of a prominent Llŷn mountain, enlarged in a second phase and reused in the medieval period. Path up from Garnfadryn village.
Hillfort on Mynydd Ystum near Aberdaron whose first phases date to the late Bronze Age; legend says the giant Odo Gawr lies under a summit cairn.
Neolithic burial chamber known as Coetan Arthur on Mynydd Cefnamwlch, near Tudweiliog in Llŷn.
Remains of a Neolithic burial chamber near Garndolbenmaen with a cup-marked rock nearby.
Neolithic chambered long cairn near Llanystumdwy, between Criccieth and Porthmadog.
Small Neolithic dolmen on the coast at Clynnog Fawr whose capstone is covered in cup-marks.
Neolithic chamber tomb in fields near Clynnog Fawr, part of the cluster of tombs on this coast.
Shallow lake beside the A5 below Tryfan; legend says Sir Bedivere threw Excalibur here after Camlann and that Tryfan is his resting place.
Glacial lake in Cwm Idwal named after Prince Idwal Foel, whose son legend says was drowned here. Popular circular path from Ogwen.
Bronze Age standing stone in the Glynllifon area near Llandwrog.
Two Neolithic portal tombs in one long cairn behind the village school, among the earliest tombs in Britain (c.4000 BC). In Cadw care, open access.
Two great Neolithic long cairns on the hillside above Dyffryn Ardudwy, with remains of chambers; reached on foot by an upland track.
Neolithic chamber with a sloping capstone amid ancient field walls near Dyffryn Ardudwy, with views over Cardigan Bay.
Pair of prehistoric stone circles on the moorland above Dyffryn Ardudwy, near the Carneddau Hengwm cairns.
Bronze Age cairn east of Talsarnau ringed by 18 slanting slate spikes like a crown, dating to the late 3rd millennium BC. Damaged by army gunnery; a remote moorland walk.
Bronze Age ring cairns and standing stones along an ancient trackway near Harlech, below Moel Goedog hillfort.
Leaning 3.1m Bronze Age slab near Trawsfynydd; folklore says the giant Idris hurled it from Cadair Idris.
Small embanked stone circle on the hills above Barmouth, bearing King Arthur's name.
The 'Irishmen's church' - a small stone circle on the uplands above Tywyn.
Standing stone near the Cregennen lakes below Cadair Idris, National Trust land with a car park and walks.
Bird Rock, a 258m crag in the Dysynni valley and the largest inland cormorant colony in Wales; its top carries a two-phase Iron Age fort.
Long narrow Iron Age fort on a 365m ridge north-east of Llandderfel near Bala, with its main entrance at the north-east end.
'Bearded Lake' above Aberdyfi, home in legend to the afanc that Arthur dragged out, and to green-clad fairies with white cattle. Reached by a hill path.
Stone near Llyn Barfog bearing a hoof-shaped hollow, said to be the print of Arthur's horse as it hauled the afanc from the lake. Marked by a slate sign.
Series of three waterfalls in a wooded gorge near Tywyn, reached on foot from Dolgoch station on the Talyllyn Railway.
Severn-Cotswold style long cairn above Betws-y-Coed with a passage and twin chambers, one still roofed by its capstone; once used as a stable. Cadw site.
Classic little Neolithic dolmen beside the old track near Rowen; its names mean 'bard's stone', 'shepherd's hut' and 'greyhound's kennel'.
Neolithic chambered tomb on the Great Orme near the tramway; the name means 'lair of the greyhound bitch'.
Stone alignment on the Great Orme whose name means 'the deer's track'.
Great Orme cave where lapidary Thomas Kendrick found a decorated horse jaw, bear-tooth beads and human bones in 1880 - some of Britain's oldest art.
Palaeolithic cave at Llandudno, protected as a scheduled monument.
The 'pass of the two stones': twin prehistoric standing stones on the old Roman road over the Carneddau between Rowen and Abergwyngregyn. Walkable green track.
Small stone circle on the moors near Bwlch y Ddeufaen, above Rowen.
Maen Crwn and Bryn Derwydd Circle
A standing stone and small stone circle on the Penmaenmawr uplands, part of the ritual landscape around the Druid's Circle.
Dolmen with a huge capstone beside a footpath overlooking the Conwy estuary near Llansanffraid Glan Conwy.
Iron Age fort on top of Conwy Mountain containing a smaller, more heavily defended fort within it; occupied from about the 6th century BC.
Small fort on a hillock on the eastern slopes of Tal-y-Fan above Rowen, little investigated.
Hill above Rhos-on-Sea with a massive limestone-walled hillfort on top and the ruin of Llys Euryn below; local nature reserve.
Wooded hill above Abergele (Tan-y-Gopa) with an Iron Age fort and caves used by rare lesser horseshoe bats; Woodland Trust land.
Large limestone hillfort above Llanddulas, near Abergele.
Small hillfort on the Great Orme above Llandudno.
Falls about 25 feet high on the Afon Crafnant in Trefriw village, left by Ice Age glaciers that cut the side valley short.
Waterfall, nicknamed the Grey Mare's Tail, just off the B5106 near Gwydir Castle, fed by a stream running out of the Gwydir Forest mines.
Lake in the Gwydir Forest linked to the bard Taliesin, with a memorial to him by the water; the lane comes from Trefriw or Llanrwst.
Early medieval holy well at St George near Abergele, once used to bless horses. Scheduled monument.
'The Giant's Grave' - an Iron Age promontory fort at the end of the Cefn Meiriadog ridge west of St Asaph, over the Elwy valley.
Four linked caves in limestone cliffs above the Elwy, where Palaeolithic tools and animal bones were dug out from the 1830s. Reached on a woodland path.
Valley-side caves above the Vale of Clwyd where stone tools were found with mammoth and woolly rhino bones in the 1880s.
Lowest of the Clwydian Range chain of hillforts, on a 200m summit over the Wheeler valley near Bodfari.
Oval Iron Age fort on a western spur of the Clwydian Range above Llanbedr Dyffryn Clwyd, overlooking the Vale.
Iron Age fort on Llantysilio Mountain north-west of Llangollen, part of the Heather and Hillforts project.
Hillfort above Dyserth at the north end of the Clwydian Range, partly quarried away; wide views to Snowdonia.
Stone block in St Peter's Square, Ruthin, on which King Arthur is said to have beheaded Huail, brother of Gildas.
Circle of at least 19 stones in a heather clearing in Clocaenog Forest, near the fallen 3.4m Maen Llwyd.
Bronze Age kerb circle of thirteen fallen stones near Llandrillo in the Dee valley.
Two Neolithic cairns at Cefn Meiriadog dug in the mid-1800s, revealing crouched burials in stone cists.
Curving Telford weir on the Dee above Llangollen that feeds the canal; a short walk from Berwyn station.
Huge Neolithic cairn on Gop Hill above Trelawnyd, the second-largest prehistoric mound in Britain after Silbury Hill; caves below held Neolithic burials.
Tallest wheel-headed cross in Britain (3.4m), carved around the 11th century and standing in a field near Whitford. Cadw site.
Five stones in a ring completed by oaks in Penbedw Park near Nannerch - possibly an 18th-century folly - with a genuine Bronze Age standing stone nearby.
1.9m Bronze Age standing stone near Treuddyn, possibly once set in a burial mound.
Hillfort on a ridge near Hope above the Alyn valley.
