Great red sandstone outcrop on Thurstaston Common; folklore makes it a Viking altar to Thor or a stone he hurled, and children once danced round it.
Sandstone carvings of a sun goddess and a horse near Bidston Observatory, thought to be Norse-Irish work of around AD 1000; the goddess faces midsummer sunrise.
Six Neolithic sandstone slabs with cup-and-ring and spiral carvings from a lost burial monument, now displayed at Calderstones Park, Liverpool.
Bronze Age cup-marked standing stone at Booker Avenue, Liverpool; its grooves are said to come from archers sharpening arrows.
Iron Age fort known as Maiden Castle on Bickerton Hill, on the Sandstone Trail, one of only seven in Cheshire; National Trust heathland.
Iron Age promontory fort near Kelsall, part of a small cluster with Eddisbury; a bronze palstave was found here.
Largest of the shattered quartzite tors on the Stiperstones ridge, steeped in Devil folklore; Wild Edric is said to ride here when England is threatened.
Iron Age fort on the 407m summit of the Wrekin; legend says the hill is earth dropped by a giant who meant to bury Shrewsbury.
Oval circle of low stones near Chirbury, one of only two surviving circles in this border area with Mitchell's Fold.
Spectacular oval multi-ramparted Iron Age fort on Sunnyhill between Clun and Bishop's Castle, managed by Forestry England with a car park nearby.
Single-ramparted late Bronze Age/early Iron Age fort on a spur of Brown Clee Hill.
Iron Age fort on the 533m summit of Titterstone Clee, unusual for its stone-block walls, alongside Bronze Age cairns and old quarries.
Small six-stone circle just west of Stanton Moor near Birchover; on private farmland with no public access.
Four tall survivors of a circle on Harthill Moor near Elton, one with cup marks, close to Robin Hood's Stride.
Gritstone outcrop with two pinnacles, also called Mock Beggar's Mansion, beside the old Portway near Elton; a medieval crucifix is carved in the nearby Hermit's Cave.
Big cup-and-ring marked boulder on Stanton Moor, later inscribed to the Duke of Wellington; on private land.
Embanked stone circle among about 80 cairns on Ramsley Moor near Baslow.
Largest embanked stone circle in Derbyshire, on Eyam Moor; off the paths but on open-access land.
Bronze Age circle on Moscar Moor above Ladybower reservoir, known as the Seven Stones of Hordron.
High Neolithic tomb on Taddington Moor with two paved chambers; at least twelve skeletons were found here.
Tree-capped hill near Pikehall holding Derbyshire's largest Neolithic chambered tomb and two Bronze Age barrows.
Big barrow 300m from Arbor Low, a Neolithic oval mound topped by a Bronze Age round barrow with a cremation cist.
Unusual square Bronze Age barrow on Beeley Moor above Chatsworth; English Heritage guardianship, beside the moorland walk.
Cliff-girt promontory on Hathersage Moor walled off by an ancient rampart, often read as an Iron Age fort though its date is uncertain.
Hillfort above Monsal Dale, hastily built; excavations in 2011 found a mass grave of women and children from a massacre.
Limestone show cave on the edge of Buxton named after a 15th-century outlaw; Bronze Age and Roman-period finds came from inside.
Castleton show cave where the rare banded Blue John stone is still mined in small amounts; guided tours.
Rock arch in the Delph at Eyam where the rector held open-air services during the 1665 plague; a commemoration service is still held there.
Small pool on top of the Roaches said to hold a water spirit or mermaid, sometimes called Jenny Greenteeth, who lures walkers in.
Castleton cave reached by boat along a flooded miners' level to a cavern with a 'Bottomless Pit' and underground lake.
Neolithic chambered long cairn on Anglezarke Moor above Chorley, with the slabs of its burial chamber still visible.
Large prehistoric round barrow on Anglezarke Moor, lined up between Great Hill and Pikestones.
Body-shaped graves cut into the headland rock beside the ruined Saxon St Patrick's Chapel at Heysham.
Limestone hill near Carnforth topped by a small multi-ramparted hillfort; nature reserves with views over Morecambe Bay.
Iron Age hillfort with triple ramparts on a hill between Nelson and Colne.
Damaged stone circle on moorland near Turton, smashed by a farmer in the 1870s; once claimed as a druid site.
Double ring of stones on Birkrigg Common south of Ulverston, known as the Druids' Temple; cremations were found under its cobbles.
Five circles on the moor above Boot in Eskdale, the largest (Brat's Hill) holding five cairns; National Trust.
Large widely spaced circle on Elva Hill north of Bassenthwaite Lake, reached by footpath from the road.
Restored circle of twelve stones near Seascale, close to Sellafield, re-erected after being buried by a farmer in 1820.
Small granite circle beside the fell road from Ennerdale Bridge, 'restored' in concrete in 1925.
Kerb circle near Long Meg with one stone carved with concentric rings and a spiral.
Oval of fallen pink granite stones near Orton, partly blasted in 1862.
Neolithic henge at Eamont Bridge near Penrith, its Arthurian name long attached; free English Heritage site.
Massive Neolithic henge with banks of river cobbles and a lone standing stone inside, near Eamont Bridge; English Heritage, free.
Two standing stones with cup-and-ring marks at the foot of Black Combe, in a field off the A595.
Shaft cave near Storth, also called the Fairy Cave, where excavations found prehistoric human and animal remains.
Cave at Great Urswick with burials from the Neolithic and Bronze Age and human bone dated to about 11,000 years ago.
Oval stone-walled Iron Age fort crowning Carrock Fell in the northern Lake District.
Small craggy Borrowdale fell whose summit is thought to have been an ancient hillfort, partly quarried away.
The Lake District's highest waterfall, about 170 feet, hidden in a gorge on Red Pike above Crummock Water.
Cascade from Watendlath tumbling into Borrowdale near Derwentwater, possibly the Derwennydd falls of an old Welsh lullaby.
One of the Lake District's highest falls, in Seathwaite above Borrowdale.
England's highest cascade above ground, falling 650 feet from the Howgill Fells near Sedbergh.
Boulders in the Irthing Gorge famous for marriage proposals, where Walter Scott is said to have proposed in 1797.
